content: Have you ever wondered why your phone charger gets warm after being plugged in for a long time, or how an electric iron becomes hot enough to press clothes without any fire?
Why do you think electrical devices produce heat even when they are only meant to produce light or do mechanical work?

content.title: Electrons Moving Through a Wire
content.description: Animation showing electrons flowing through a wire and colliding with atoms, producing heat energy due to resistance.

content: This happens because of the **Heating Effect of Electric Current**. When an electric current passes through a high resistance wire (like nichrome), the electrical energy is converted into heat energy.

question: Which of the following devices works primarily on the heating effect of electric current?

content: Think of three other appliances in your home that get hot when switched on. How would life be different if we couldn't use the heating effect of electricity?
This concept is connected to **Resistance** (how much a material opposes current). Later, you will learn how this same heating effect is used in electrical fuses to protect our homes from fires!
Design a simple safety device on paper that would break a circuit if the wire gets too hot. What material would you use and why?

Imagine a giant crane at a junkyard picking up a whole car using just a flat metal plate, without any hooks. How can a piece of metal become a super-strong magnet at the flick of a switch, and then drop the car when the switch is turned off?
If electricity can create heat, could it also create a magnetic pull? What do you think happens to a compass needle if you place it near a wire carrying electric current?

content.title: Oersted's Experiment
content.description: Animation showing a compass needle deflecting when an electric current is passed through a nearby wire, demonstrating the magnetic field.

content: This phenomenon is known as the **Magnetic Effect of Electric Current**. A coil of wire with a current flowing through it acts like a magnet, and it is called an **Electromagnet**.

question: What happens to an electromagnet when the electric current is switched off?

content: If you were to build your own electromagnet using a nail, wire, and battery, how could you make it strong enough to pick up 50 paperclips instead of just 5?
The magnetic effect of electric current is the foundational principle behind electric motors, which are used in everything from electric cars to the fans in your house.

Your challenge: You need to separate iron nails from a pile of plastic beads, but you don't have a permanent magnet. Write down the steps and materials you need to build a temporary magnet to solve this problem.
